## Summary

I traced untrusted inputs to dangerous sinks across the OAuth service and confirmed **2 exploitable findings** (both verified at runtime against the actual code):

### CRITICAL — Authentication bypass (`src/oauth/token.js` + `src/oauth/jwks.js`)
`verifyExternalToken` selects the JWT-verification key URL from `header.jku` (attacker-controlled token header). The only guard is a bare `String(url).startsWith('https://keys.example.test')` prefix check, which is bypassed by `https://keys.example.test@evil.com/...` (resolves to `evil.com`) or `https://keys.example.test.evil.com/...`. Combined with `redirect: 'follow'`, an attacker hosts their own JWKS, signs a token, and gets it accepted → full auth bypass.

### HIGH — Authorization redirect_uri interception (`src/oauth/register.js`)
`validateRedirect` uses `redirectUri.startsWith(client.baseUrl)` to authorize where OAuth codes/tokens are sent. The same prefix flaw accepts `https://portal.example.test.evil.com/cb` / `...@evil.com/cb`, redirecting user codes to an attacker host. The repo ships an unused exact-match helper (`exact-redirect.js`), confirming this is the unintended weaker path.

### Excluded as non-exploitable (avoiding false positives)
- `safe-jwks.js`, `pkce.js`, `state.js`, `config.js`, `logging.js`, `client-repo.js` — safe/correct.
- The `exact-redirect.js` query-string gap and `state.js` length-mismatch throw were excluded as pattern-only (no exploitable caller context).
